summary:
Udmurtia has produced no division-specific transgender evidence in the available sources. A visitor to the republic of Udmurtia stands under the national framework of Russia as it operates countrywide, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework against which this division is assessed.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the UK Home Office note records that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in November 2023.

The expanded 'propaganda' statute criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia, with 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reaching up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office note contains no information specific to Udmurtia beyond the national framework, so the assessment for this republic rests entirely on countrywide Russian law and enforcement data.

Human Rights Watch's article on the extremism designation likewise contains no division-specific detail; the 101 convictions and 98 administrative cases it records are national figures that underpin the national score this division is assessed at.

Enforcement patterns documented in Moscow and St Petersburg indicate that major urban centres have been the primary sites of club raids and extremism prosecutions, but the legal instruments applied are national statutes in force throughout the country, including Udmurtia.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals across Russia were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Udmurtia-specific reporting on transgender individuals, local enforcement actions, or regional authorities' conduct toward LGBT+ people was located in the available sources; the division-level picture is unresolved rather than absent.

Whether Udmurtia's regional interior ministry or courts have pursued extremism or article 20.3 charges at rates comparable to Moscow or St Petersburg is not sourced here.

Local access to documentation services, healthcare facilities, and any informal support networks within Izhevsk or other Udmurtian cities is not covered by the inventory and remains unverified.
